new_text: The dressing bell broke up the company. It was not until after dinner that I saw him again; he then seemed perfectly at ease. But I liked his face even less than before: it struck me as being at once restless and lifeless. His eye wandered without purpose: this gave him a strange look unlike any I had seen before. For a handsome and not unpleasant-looking man, he repelled me strongly. There was no force in that smooth-skinned, oval face; no firmness in that hooked nose and small, red mouth; no thought on the low, even forehead; no will in that blank, brown eye.

new_text: I wondered what they would do the first evening a change of entertainment was proposed. They spoke of "playing charades," but in my ignorance I did not know what that meant. The servants were called in, the dining room tables wheeled away, the lights rearranged, and chairs placed in a semicircle facing the arch. While Mr. Rochester and the other gentlemen directed these changes, the ladies ran up and down stairs ringing for their maids. Mrs. Fairfax was called upon to report what the house could supply in the way of shawls, dresses, and draperies of any kind. Certain wardrobes on the third floor were ransacked, and their contents—brocaded and hooped petticoats, satin sack gowns, black silk gowns, lace caps, and the like—were brought down in armloads by the maids. A selection was made, and the chosen items were carried to the boudoir off the drawing room.

new_text: "No—some inexplicable one. In short, I believe you have been trying to draw me out—or draw me in. You have been talking nonsense to make me talk nonsense. It is hardly fair, sir."
